prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, enabling atomic time and frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a concrete, nameable invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects for many neutral atoms at once, and Ye's strontium clocks showed what that buys, fractional uncertainty and stability near 1e-18. The physics is atomic structure and light-atom interaction of the kind I calculate for a living, so I can judge that the magic-wavelength condition is a real and non-trivial idea and not a refinement of the single-ion approach. It is reproduced by many independent laboratories, compared across continents, and underpins the coming redefinition of the second, tests of constant variation, relativistic geodesy and dark-matter searches. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two credited names that map exactly onto invention and demonstration, with no one forced out by the three-person limit. The prior prizes for the frequency comb (2005) and ion control (2012) do not cover neutral-atom lattice clocks.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this can be read as a further step in a metrology lineage already rewarded in 2005 and 2012, and that the headline fundamental-physics payoff (redefinition of the second, new-physics searches) is still largely prospective rather than delivered. Ye's work spans several platforms, and the early ytterbium and mercury lattice work and the Al+ ion clocks could also claim credit, so a two-name prize invites questions about who was left out. A committee that weights discovery of a new phenomenon over invention of an instrument would put the topological or moire candidates ahead.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator first as a clean prediction followed by a decisive observation that opened a whole field, and treats it as overdue rather than premature, while ranking the lattice clock only sixth.
responses.response: I agree that the Z2 insulator is a strong, mature and very influential case and I ranked it third. Where I differ is on the weight of the unresolved attribution: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan sits outside the credited names, and Danielsson's own opening acknowledges that the allocation is a real question. The 2016 prize also covered topological phases, so the novelty is partly absorbed. The lattice clock has no comparable credit hole. I would not call Danielsson's point wrong, but a prize that cannot be allocated cleanly is, for me, less ready than one that can.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as the clearest case of better measurement opening new physics, and regards Katori and Ye as sufficient credit, with the Hall, Hansch and Wineland prizes not conflicting.
responses.response: I largely share this view, but I want to qualify the claim that better measurement has already opened new physics. What has been delivered is a capability: 1e-18 comparisons and a path to redefining the second. The tests of constants and dark matter so far set limits. I think the citation should therefore stress the invention and its realisation, not discoveries made with the clocks, which keeps the case where the evidence is strongest. I also think Kroll understates the Ludlow, Yb and Al+ clock communities who will ask why the prize is not broader.

responses.point: Olsson ranks the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize first and the lattice clock only sixth, noting overlap with the frequency-comb and ion-trap prizes and the unfinished SI redefinition.
responses.response: The overlap concern is serious and I considered it, but I do not think it holds. The comb prize gave a way to count optical cycles and the ion prize gave control of single trapped particles; the lattice clock combines a different physical idea, magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, with a different error budget and stability regime. The pending redefinition is a timing question, not a doubt about the science, because the accuracy is verified by independent comparisons now.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first and Kane-Mele-Molenkamp second, and ranks optical-lattice quantum simulation fifth, noting that five credited names leave no clean three-person subset.
responses.response: I agree on the difficulty with the optical-lattice simulation candidate, and it is why I keep it as an alternative and not my lead despite ranking it second: Zoller, Bloch, Greiner, Cirac and Dalibard all have strong claims. Its payoff to date is largely methodological, as I said in my own opening, and Cirac and Zoller recur in the trapped-ion candidate, which complicates any combination. That is a reason for me to prefer the cleaner lattice-clock credit.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that lattice clocks are distinct from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes, or reads them as a continuation.
Whether Ye's platform spread, and the early Yb and Hg lattice work or Al+ ion clocks, make a two-name credit contestable.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and three-dimensional topological insulator credit questions can be settled well enough to put B044 ahead.
I rely on my recollection of priority details between Katori's proposal and parallel ideas, which I have not verified from the files supplied.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the lattice-clock candidate: my documented collaborators (Lund attosecond group, ETH Zurich, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Indelicato) are not among Katori or Ye. As a theoretical atomic physicist I am professionally close to the optical-clock field in general, but have no documented relationship with the credited individuals.
